name: Puerta de la Trinidad, Badajoz
coord_source: https://www.castillosnet.org/monumento.php?r=BA-CAS-054-PTR&seo=puerta-de-la-trinidad (location text: start of Ronda del Pilar by Puente de San Roque; point placed from that description, not a published coordinate)
text: On 14 August 1936 Lt-Col. Juan Yagüe's Army of Africa columns stormed Badajoz, defended by Col. Ildefonso Puigdendolas with loyal troops and several thousand militia. The breach assault at the Puerta de la Trinidad was the bloodiest action of the day: the 16th Company of the Legion's 4th Bandera charged through machine-gun fire at the gate and was almost wiped out before the walls were carried, while Castejón's men broke in further south. Badajoz's fall joined the Nationalist zones of the south and north and opened the road up the Tagus valley towards Madrid. What followed inside the city became one of the war's most notorious episodes of repression.
look: The 17th-century gate and walls survive at the northeast corner of the old town, beside the Rivillas stream and the Puente de San Roque.
plan: Free, street-side, any time; combine on foot with the former bullring site (Palacio de Congresos) about 15 minutes away along the Ronda del Pilar.
disputed: Legion losses at the gate vary by source (from about 20 dead and 22 wounded to 76 of about 90 men of the 16th Company).

name: Former bullring (Palacio de Congresos) – Badajoz massacre memorial
text: After the city fell, Nationalist troops and Falangists rounded up militiamen, Popular Front supporters and people found with bruised shoulders from rifle recoil. Many were held in the bullring and shot there and elsewhere; bodies were burned and buried at the San Juan cemetery. Reports by Mário Neves, Jay Allen and other foreign journalists made 'Badajoz' known worldwide. The bullring was demolished in 2000 and the Palacio de Congresos 'Manuel Rojas' (2006) was built on the site within the San Roque bastion. After years of controversy a small permanent memorial display, 'Memorial Badajoz 1936', was installed in the lobby in 2021.
look: A modern congress hall on the site of the ring; in the lobby, information panels, a display case and audiovisual material on the massacre, plus a model of Blanca Muñoz's sculpture 'Eclíptica' that stands outside.
plan: The lobby is accessible when the building is open for events or office hours; check with the Palacio de Congresos (tel. 924 939 000). Outside, the sculpture can be seen any time.
disputed: Death toll strongly disputed: contemporary press reported 1,800–4,000 killed in the city; later historians (e.g. Francisco Espinosa) give several thousand victims in the city over the following months, while some revisionist authors argue for a few hundred. Whether mass shootings took place inside the bullring itself is also debated by the revisionist side.

name: Puente Romano, Mérida (fall of Mérida)
text: Mérida was the key road and rail junction between the Nationalist south and north. Around 2,600 militiamen and loyal forces held the Guadiana line against columns under Asensio, Castejón and Tella. On 10 August the Legion's 5th Bandera rushed the 2,000-year-old Roman bridge, which the defenders had mined; the charges were not fired (Nationalist accounts credit Cmdr. Luis Alarcón de la Lastra with disarming them) and the troops broke into the city. Mérida's capture linked Seville with Mola's northern zone. Mass detentions followed: the bullring, the Santo Domingo convent and the barracks became prison camps, and executions took place at the cemetery wall.
look: The Roman bridge (now pedestrian) over the Guadiana, where the assault crossed; in the town, the town hall on Plaza de España and a memorial at the municipal cemetery to the victims of the repression.
plan: Free, always open; walk the bridge from the Alcazaba end (10 min). The cemetery memorial is a short drive north of the centre.
disputed: Casualties of the fighting are not reliably known; numbers for the subsequent repression in Mérida vary between studies.

name: Almendralejo – Purificación church tower & memorial
text: On the drive north from Seville, Asensio's and Castejón's columns entered Almendralejo on 7 August 1936. About fifty militiamen barricaded themselves in the tower of the parish church of Nuestra Señora de la Purificación and held out for a week against artillery, explosives and smoke before surrendering; they were then shot. The town suffered heavy repression, including the killing of a number of women. A memorial in the municipal cemetery, unveiled in November 2023, names 462 victims from Almendralejo and 252 from other towns killed nearby. Earlier, under Republican control, several right-wing prisoners had also been killed in the town.
look: The tall church tower on Plaza de España, still showing its role in the siege only through local accounts; the new memorial wall in the municipal cemetery.
plan: The church exterior is free on Plaza de España; the cemetery lies at the edge of town (usual cemetery hours).
disputed: Numbers killed after the capture vary widely: some accounts give 28 on entry, Portuguese journalists reported up to 1,000; the 2023 memorial names 714 victims (town + other localities). The number of right-wing victims killed earlier in the town is also debated.

name: Palacio de los Golfines de Arriba, Cáceres (Franco HQ 1936)
text: From 26 August 1936 Franco set up his headquarters in this Renaissance palace in Cáceres old town, directing the Army of Africa's advance up the Tagus towards Talavera and Toledo. He stayed some 38 days; in late September, while based here, he was chosen by his fellow generals as commander-in-chief and head of the rebel state, before the formal proclamation in Burgos on 1 October and his move to Salamanca. The palace is one of few places that shows how the rebel command was improvised in private buildings of provincial towns.
look: The fine Renaissance façade in the walled old town (a UNESCO site). A Francoist commemorative plaque has been the subject of removal requests by memory associations.
plan: Privately owned (hospitality use); view from the street. Easy to combine with a walk through the Ciudad Monumental.

name: Castuera concentration camp (La Verilleja)
text: When the Republican Army of Extremadura surrendered at the end of March 1939, Nationalist authorities built a camp on the La Verilleja estate about 3 km from Castuera, in the La Serena district. For about a year it held thousands of Republican soldiers and civilians awaiting classification and trial; many were taken out and shot, some reportedly at nearby mine shafts. The camp was laid out with a perimeter ditch, streets of barracks, a central square with a cross, latrines and washrooms. In 2009 it was declared a Bien de Interés Cultural (historic site) — one of the best-preserved Francoist camp layouts in Spain.
look: On the ground: the perimeter ditch, main gate area, paved camp streets, barrack foundations and the cement base of the cross; memorial markers placed by the memory association.
plan: Site is within private farmland; access is along a marked track from the Castuera–Benquerencia road — ask at Castuera tourist office or the Asociación Memorial Campo de Concentración de Castuera about access and annual commemorative walks.
disputed: Prisoner numbers range from 8,000–9,000 (Julián Chaves) to 15,000–20,000 in other estimates; the number executed is not established. Mapcarta's point (from Wikidata) should be checked on site against the BIC boundary.

name: Campillo de Llerena – Civil War Museum & Italian cemetery
text: Campillo de Llerena lay just behind the Nationalist line on the static southern Extremadura front. In 1937 Italian units of the mixed Italo-Spanish 'Flechas Azules' brigade, based here, created a war cemetery for their dead. The restored Cementerio de los Italianos and the town's Civil War museum — Extremadura's first — form one complex. The museum, expanded in 2023, recreates a trench and bunker and displays material from the fortifications of south-eastern Badajoz, explaining life in the trenches on both sides. It is presented as a place of remembrance for victims of both sides.
look: The walled Italian cemetery outside the village; in town (Plaza Cívica 1) the museum with a reconstructed trench and bunker and finds from the front.
plan: The museum website recently stated it was closed for renovation — phone the town hall (924 770 131) before travelling. The cemetery is about 1.3 km north of the village centre.

name: Valle de la Serena – Republican defence line (La Serena pocket)
text: From late 1936 the Republic held a large salient in eastern Badajoz, the 'La Serena pocket'. Along the Guadámez valley Republican engineers and local masons built concrete-and-brick machine-gun posts linked by zigzag trenches; one carries the inscription 'AÑO 1937'. In July 1938 Queipo de Llano's Army of the South attacked, taking Castuera, Campanario and Villanueva de la Serena and cutting off much of the pocket, while the Republican front fell back to the Zújar and Guadiana. Unlike the famous fronts, these works are almost untouched and little visited.
look: Small round and square fortines (about 3 × 3 m inside, four firing slits) and stretches of trench at Cañada Honda and Los Palancares, controlling the roads to Puebla de la Reina and Don Benito.
plan: On farmland off local roads; no signage — go with a local guide or the 'guerracivilenbadajoz' route notes, wear boots, respect livestock gates. Coordinates are the village centre only.
